summary: Business With Brian argues a memory dip like this comes only once a decade, after tech sold off hard at the end of the week and memory took some of the hardest hits. His canary is SK Hynix: almost pure memory, hit by a Chinese rival's announcement and exposed to a helium supply cut, yet it just reported one of the best quarters in its history, which he reads as proof the scare headlines are noise. The core thesis is a structural shift: customers now pay upfront, with Micron holding about $12.7B of non-cancellable customer cash, so makers hold the cards while demand outruns supply. His calls are all conditional buys, in pieces by dollar-cost averaging on the way down, only while the shortage holds: Micron (only US maker of both HBM and DRAM, 3-year forecast about $2,500 per $1,000), Western Digital and Seagate (hard-drive 'warehouse' pricing power, about $3,000 each), SanDisk (pure-play flash, just over $2,500, with an 8-for-1 split on 20 Nov) and Rambus (the traffic-directing chip on about 45% of new server sticks, about $1,600). He warns that if memory turns like past cycles it could be worse than even his bear case, advises against the SK Hynix ADR at a roughly 48% premium, and sketches ETF routes via DRAM, EWY and SOXX. Note: captions garble some company names; one segment is a paid Mayfair Gold sponsorship, not a call.
